'''Tevian Dray''' (born March 17, 1956) is an American mathematician who has worked in [[general relativity]], [[mathematical physics]], [[geometry]], and both [[science education|science]] and [[mathematics education|mathematics]] education.  He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2010.

He has primarily worked in the area of classical general relativity.  His research results include confirmation of the existence of solutions of [[Einstein's equation]] containing [[gravitational radiation]], the use of [[computer algebra]] to classify exact solutions of Einstein's equation, an analysis of a class of gravitational shock waves (including one of the few known exact [[two-body problem|2-body solutions]] in general relativity), and the study of [[metric signature|signature]] change, a possible model for the [[Big Bang]].  More recently, his work has focused on applications of the [[octonions]] to the theory of fundamental particles.

He was a graduate student under [[Rainer K. Sachs]] at [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley]], where he received his [[Ph.D.]] in 1981, although much of his dissertation research was done in collaboration with [[Abhay Ashtekar]]. The context of his dissertation, titled ''The Asymptotic Structure of a Family of Einstein-Maxwell Solutions'' focused on families of [[spacetimes]] which describe accelerating black holes, and which contain gravitational radiation. This demonstrated the existence of exact radiating solutions to the Einstein field equations.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.oregonstate.edu/~tevian/thesis/ |title=Tevian Dray's Dissertation }}</ref>

He is currently a professor of mathematics at [[Oregon State University]]. In addition to his ongoing work in mathematical physics, he has made significant contributions in science education, where he directs the Vector Calculus Bridge Project,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.oregonstate.edu/bridge |title = Bridging the Vector Calculus Gap}}</ref> an attempt to teach vector calculus the way it is used by scientists and engineers, and is part of the development team of the Paradigms Project,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://physics.oregonstate.edu/portfolioswiki |title=Start – Portfolios Wiki}}</ref> a complete restructuring of the undergraduate physics major around several core "paradigms".  He has written a book<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://physics.oregonstate.edu/coursewikis/GSR/bookinfo |title = Bookinfo – Geometry of Special Relativity}}</ref> on special relativity and a sequel on general relativity using differential forms,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://physics.oregonstate.edu/coursewikis/DFGGR/bookinfo | title=Differential Forms and the Geometry of General Relativity}}</ref> and is coauthor of ''[[The Geometry of the Octonions]]'', released in 2015.<ref name=oct>Reviews of ''The Geometry of the Octonions'':
* {{citation|title=none|journal=Mathematical Reviews|first=Alberto|last=Elduque|mr=3361898|year=2015}}
* {{citation|title=Review|journal=J. Geom. Symmetry Phys.|volume=39|year=2015|pages=99–101|first=Danail|last=Brezov|url=https://www.emis.de/journals/JGSP/jgsp_files/vol39/Brezov_rew.pdf}}
* {{citation|title=Review|journal=MAA Reviews|first=Mark|last=Hunacek|date=June 2015|url=https://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/the-geometry-of-the-octonions}}</ref>

In 2017 he received a [[Deborah and Franklin Haimo Awards for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics|Deborah and Franklin Haimo Award for Distinguished College or University Teaching of Mathematics]].<ref name=web />
